instructions: Rinse the 1 1/2 cups rice in a pot, swirling it and draining it until the water runs mostly clear. Add 2 1/4 cups water and bring it to a boil over high heat. Cover, turn the heat to low and cook for 12 minutes. Leave it covered off the heat until the paneer is done.

Meanwhile, cut the paneer into 1 inch cubes. Slice the onion into petals and cut the bell pepper into 1 inch pieces. Chop the scallions and set 3 tbsp aside for the top. Mince 3 of the garlic cloves, and grate the last clove and the ginger. Slice the green chili into a small bowl for the table.

In a bowl, whisk 1/3 cup of the cornstarch, the 3 tbsp flour, the grated garlic and ginger, 1/2 tsp Kashmiri chili powder, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/3 cup water into a smooth, thick batter.

In a small bowl, stir together the 2 1/2 tbsp soy sauce, 2 tbsp ketchup, 2 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp chili sauce, 1/4 tsp Kashmiri chili powder, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 1/4 tsp salt, the last 2 tsp cornstarch and 1/4 cup water until there are no lumps.
Pour the 3/4 cup oil into a 12 inch skillet and heat it over medium-high for 2 minutes, until a drop of batter sizzles right away.

Toss the paneer in the batter. Lift out a few cubes at a time, let the extra drip off, and lay them in the oil in a single layer. Fry in two batches, 2 to 3 minutes per side, until golden and crisp. Transfer them to a plate.
Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the oil into a heatproof bowl and set the pan over high heat. Add the minced garlic and 6 tbsp of the scallions and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the onion and bell pepper and stir over high heat for 1 minute. They should stay crisp.
Stir the sauce again and pour it in. Cook for 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until it's glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon.
Add the paneer and toss for 30 seconds to coat it.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Fluff the rice with a fork. Serve the paneer over the rice, scattered with the 3 tbsp scallions, with the sliced green chili on the side.
method_notes: Hebbar's Kitchen (the lead) coats the paneer in a cornflour and plain flour batter, fries it until crisp, then tosses it with onion, capsicum, garlic, spring onion and a soy, vinegar, chili and tomato sauce thickened with a cornflour slurry. The lead is written for 3, so everything is scaled to 4. The sauce gets 1/4 cup of water instead of the lead's 2 tbsp so it coats the paneer and rice, the green chili in the sauce moves to the table, and the paneer is shallow fried in a skillet. Only the lead was readable; the other well-rated versions block the reader.
